extracted.intended_audience: attorneys, IP practitioners, and parties (complainants/respondents) involved in U.S. ITC Section 337 investigations
extracted.subtask_description: Practical/practice-oriented guidance on establishing domestic industry, proving injury, seeking temporary and permanent relief, bonding, counterclaims, Presidential review, and enforcement in U.S. International Trade Commission Section 337 investigations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domestic industry requirement (technical and economic prongs)
rubrics_metrics.description: The complainant must establish a domestic industry by satisfying both the technical and economic prongs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Domestic industry activities must be more than what a mere importer would perform; mere marketing activities may fail to constitute a domestic industry. When multiple intellectual property rights or products are at issue, the analysis can become complex and may require allocation of activities to specific patents/products, although in some cases the Commission treats multiple patents/products as a single unified domestic industry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significant investment in plant and equipment / significant employment of labor or capital (first two domestic-industry tests)
rubrics_metrics.description: One way to satisfy the domestic industry economic prong is by showing significant investment in plant and equipment or significant employment of labor or capital.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A comparative value‑added analysis is an appropriate method to evaluate these first two tests — comparing value attributable to foreign activities with value attributable to U.S. activities (see value-added analysis entry and examples such as PTI where U.S. activities produced ~34% value-added).

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantial investment in exploitation of IP (third domestic-industry test)
rubrics_metrics.description: The third test requires a finding of a 'substantial investment' in the exploitation of the intellectual property right at issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The third test examines U.S. activities in absolute terms (comparative value-added analysis should not apply to the third test). Evidence must demonstrate a sufficiently focused and concentrated effort to support a finding of substantial investment; precise accounting is not necessary but minimal expenditures and undocumented 'sweat equity' may be insufficient (example: $8,500 for prototypes and undocumented sweat equity found inadequate). Pre-complaint licensing efforts are considered but the absence of actual licenses prior to complaint is a factor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value‑added analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: A comparative 'value‑added analysis' compares the amount of value attributable to foreign activities with the value attributable to activities conducted in the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used by the Commission to assess whether U.S. activities are sufficiently significant (commonly applied to the first two domestic-industry tests). Example provided: In re Certain Male Prophylactic Devices where lubricating, foiling and testing in U.S. produced 34% value added and supported a domestic-industry finding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-complaint licensing efforts (weight and evidentiary value)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pre-complaint licensing efforts (e.g., attending trade shows, discussions with manufacturers) are considered in evaluating domestic-industry investment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A consummated license prior to filing is not a prerequisite to give weight to licensing efforts, but the absence of any actual licenses prior to a complaint is a factor the Commission will consider. Documentation/detail of licensing efforts matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domestic industry allocation when multiple IP rights/products
rubrics_metrics.description: When more than one intellectual property right or more than one product is alleged, the domestic industry analysis can become complex and may require allocation of domestic activities to specific IP rights or products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In some investigations the Commission may treat multiple patents/products as a single unified domestic industry (example: DRAMs), but that approach may not always be appropriate and complainants can be burdened with allocating activities among patents/products.

rubrics_metrics.name: Injury standard for non-patent/non-registered-IP investigations
rubrics_metrics.description: If the investigation is not based on patents, copyrights, mask works or federally registered trademarks, the complainant must prove that the alleged unfair competition or unfair acts will threaten to or actually: (1) destroy or substantially injure an industry in the United States; (2) prevent the establishment of such an industry; or (3) restrain or monopolize commerce in the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There must be a nexus between the substantial injury and the unfair act — typically by showing the domestic industry's articles and the accused imported articles compete in the same markets for the same customers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors considered in injury analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission examines each investigation on its facts and considers trends in employment, production, capacity, corresponding market shares of complainant and respondent, levels of importations, and pricing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No single factor is dispositive; factors are considered in the context of the specific industry and market.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantial injury evidentiary factors
rubrics_metrics.description: To establish whether respondent’s unfair acts will substantially injure the domestic industry, the Commission considers factors such as respondent’s volume of imports and market penetration, complainant’s lost sales, underselling by the respondent, and complainant’s declining production, profitability and sales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Federal Circuit rejects the idea that mere conceivable or speculative losses establish substantial injury — something more than speculative losses is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedures to ensure speed of Section 337 investigations (target date rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission must conclude an investigation 'at the earliest practicable time' and the ALJ must establish a target date for completion within forty‑five days from initiation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For cases with target dates of less than 15 months, the ALJ's initial determination must be issued at least 3 months before the target date; for longer cases, at least 4 months before. There are no pre-established total time limits, but target dates and accelerated schedules distinguish ITC cases from district court litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and nature of Commission remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: The remedies afforded by the Commission under Section 337 are injunctive in nature; the ITC cannot award monetary damages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remedies include: (1) general exclusion orders (forbid importation irrespective of source), (2) limited exclusion orders (affect only specified foreign manufacturers named in the complaint), (3) cease and desist orders (enjoin unlawful activities by U.S. entities), (4) temporary exclusion/cease and desist orders during the pendency of an investigation, and (5) consent orders. Violations of orders can result in forfeiture and the Commission may levy sanctions for discovery/process abuses under Rule 11 and Rule 37.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for issuing a general exclusion order (19 U.S.C. § 1337 / §321(a)(5) considerations)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission's authority to order a general exclusion is limited to persons determined to be violating Section 337 unless the Commission determines that either: (a) a general exclusion is necessary to prevent circumvention of a limited exclusion order; or (b) there is a pattern of violation and it is difficult to identify the source of infringing products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of these rigorous criteria and balancing of interests, complainants more often seek limited exclusion orders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consent order considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Before issuing a consent order, the Commission must consider the effect that a proposed consent order will have on public health and welfare, competitive conditions in the domestic economy, the production of like or directly competitive articles in the United States, and consumers in the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These public‑interest considerations can influence whether and in what form a consent order issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporary relief (four-factor equitable test)
rubrics_metrics.description: To obtain temporary relief (e.g., a temporary exclusion order) the complainant must make convincing showings on four equitable factors: (a) the complainant’s likelihood of success on the merits; (b) irreparable harm to complainant in absence of temporary relief; (c) harm, if any, to the respondent(s) if temporary relief is granted; and (d) the effect on the public interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This test mirrors the Federal Circuit's standard for preliminary injunctions; temporary relief proceedings occur on an extremely fast schedule and are relatively rare because Section 337 cases already move quickly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Irreparable harm in temporary relief context
rubrics_metrics.description: Irreparable harm must be likely to occur before the Commission can issue permanent relief and is evaluated with respect to the patents involved (not any general threat to the complainant).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is a presumption of irreparable harm when the complainant makes a strong showing of validity and continuing infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bonding rules for temporary exclusion orders
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon issuance of a temporary exclusion order, the Secretary of the Treasury establishes a bond amount under which the articles may be imported during the investigation; the amount must be 'sufficient to protect the complainant from any injury.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the Commission later finds a Section 337 violation, the respondent’s bond may be forfeited to the complainant. The Commission may alternatively require a complainant to post a bond to protect respondent interests; this is discretionary (not mandatory) and if complainant’s bond is forfeited the funds may go to the respondent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bonding rules during Presidential review (permanent relief)
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon issuance of a permanent exclusion order, the Secretary of the Treasury sets a bond amount permitting importation during the Presidential review period; the bond amount should be sufficient to protect the complainant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the exclusion order becomes final (President does not disapprove), the respondent’s bond may be forfeited to the complainant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relief against defaulting respondents
rubrics_metrics.description: If a respondent fails to respond to the complaint and Notice of Investigation without cause (defaults), the ITC shall presume the facts alleged in the complaint to be true for purposes of obtaining a remedial order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Post‑1988 amendments allow remedial orders against non‑responding respondents without the complainant presenting a prima facie case; historically complainants had to present a prima facie case even against defaulting respondents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counterclaims and removal to district court (ITC Rule 210.14(e))
rubrics_metrics.description: Respondents may assert all legal and equitable defenses and, under ITC Rule 210.14(e), may assert counterclaims, but counterclaims asserted at the Commission must be removed to the appropriate U.S. district court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Immediately after asserting a counterclaim, the respondent must file a notice of removal in a U.S. district court where venue for the counterclaim exists under 28 U.S.C. § 1391. Counterclaims related to the transaction/occurrence at issue may have district-court original jurisdiction under the GATT Act amendment. Removal does not delay or affect Commission proceedings; respondent benefits from the complaint filing date for statute-of-limitations and forum-choice considerations; filing fee may be waived in some cases. Anomalies exist (e.g., related affirmative defenses are not automatically stricken; retaliatory Section 337 complaints are not always 'counterclaims' requiring removal).

rubrics_metrics.name: Presidential review of Commission orders (60‑day review)
rubrics_metrics.description: Exclusion and cease and desist orders do not take effect immediately; the President has 60 days to disapprove an order for policy reasons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: During review respondents can avoid full impact by posting bonds set by the Commission. Presidential disapprovals are rare but have occurred for reasons such as the breadth of remedy, adverse effects on U.S. firms/trade, jurisdictional overlaps with other remedies (e.g., dumping/antidumping), or contradictions with Customs rulings. The Commission may modify orders in response to Presidential concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proceedings after a Commission order becomes final (enforcement, modification, revocation)
rubrics_metrics.description: After orders become effective, they are subject to enforcement, modification, and revocation proceedings at the Commission; the Office of Unfair Import Investigations can institute informal or formal enforcement proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Informal proceedings often involve correspondence to address compliance; formal enforcement can involve Commission complaints and publication of institution notice in the Federal Register; remedies include modifying or revoking orders, bringing civil actions in U.S. district court, or directing Customs to exclude articles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Customs enforcement and administrative remedies (post-order procedures at Customs)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission’s exclusion orders are enforced by U.S. Customs and Border Protection; Customs uses internal procedures and educates field personnel on identifying excluded products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complainants should meet with Customs after an exclusion order to discuss scope and assist in identifying infringing products. Customs can issue binding administrative rulings on whether a proposed import falls within an exclusion order; decisions to exclude shipments are made by Customs Directors and are subject to a protest filed within 90 days, with denial appealable to the U.S. Court of International Trade. Conflicts between Customs rulings and Commission orders have arisen and been litigated (example: Eaton Corp. v. United States).
